title: Levels of Biological Organization
seo_title: Grade 7 Science: Levels of Biological Organization Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Living things are organized from cells to tissues, organs, organ systems and organisms; specialized cells form tissues with special functions. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 7, Quarter 2: Life Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Life Science): specialized cells and tissues, organs and organ systems, the digestive and respiratory systems, the circulatory system and plant tissues and organs. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
key_sub: Organ systems work together to keep the body alive.
body_html:
How to think about it

Cells with the same job form a tissue. Animals have four tissue types: epithelial (covers), connective (supports, such as bone and blood), muscle (moves) and nerve (signals). Tissues form organs such as the stomach, and organs work together in systems.

The digestive system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients; the respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide; the circulatory system carries them around the body. Plants have dermal, ground and vascular tissue; their organs are roots, stems, leaves and flowers, organized into the root system and the shoot system.

Example

Put in order: organ, cell, organ system, tissue.

Smallest first

Answer: cell, tissue, organ, organ system

Example

Which two systems work together to get oxygen to the muscles?

One takes in oxygen, one carries it.

Answer: respiratory and circulatory

Common mistakes

  • Calling blood an organ: it is a connective tissue.
  • Thinking organ systems work alone.
  • Saying plants have no tissues.

faq.q: Why are red blood cells specialized?
faq.a: They have no nucleus and are full of hemoglobin, so they carry as much oxygen as possible.
It carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a red blood cell?
c: no nucleus and a biconcave shape
items.e: A red blood cell has no nucleus and a biconcave shape: more room for hemoglobin and a larger surface area to take up oxygen.

items.q: Which tissue matches this description: the lining of the stomach and intestine, with tall cells?
items.e: Columnar epithelium: the lining of the stomach and intestine, with tall cells.

items.q: At which level of organization is the circulatory system?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: At which level of organization is the shoot system of a plant?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a xylem vessel?
c: no nucleus and a biconcave shape
no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
items.e: A xylem vessel has no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls: an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support.

items.q: Which tissue matches this description: the wall of the heart?
items.e: Cardiac muscle: the wall of the heart.

items.q: At which level of organization is the digestive system?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: At which level of organization is the kidney?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which cell has no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls, giving an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support?
c: a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes
items.e: Each specialized cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: At which level of organization is xylem tissue?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a root hair cell?
c: no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
no nucleus and a biconcave shape
items.e: A root hair cell has a long, narrow extension: a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes?
c: no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body
items.e: A pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes has a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body: many proteins made and packaged for secretion.

items.q: A pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes has a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body. How does this help it?
c: a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts
a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma
energy to swim to the egg
many proteins made and packaged for secretion
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which cell has many chloroplasts, giving more light absorbed for photosynthesis?
items.e: Each specialized cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: Which connective tissue has a fluid matrix?
items.e: Plasma is its matrix.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a palisade mesophyll cell?
c: a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body
items.e: A palisade mesophyll cell has many chloroplasts: more light absorbed for photosynthesis.

items.q: A red blood cell has no nucleus and a biconcave shape. How does this help it?
c: energy to swim to the egg
a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma
more room for hemoglobin and a larger surface area to take up oxygen
many proteins made and packaged for secretion
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Where is blood found, or what does it do?
c: the walls of blood vessels and air sacs of lungs
transporting substances round the body in a fluid matrix
items.e: Blood: transporting substances round the body in a fluid matrix.

items.q: At which level of organization is a leaf?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Where is tendon found, or what does it do?
c: connecting a skeletal muscle to a bone
connecting a bone to another bone
items.e: Tendon: connecting a skeletal muscle to a bone.

items.q: What level is made of many tissues working together?
items.e: Many tissues make up an organ.

items.q: Which organ system does the blood vessels belong to?
items.e: The blood vessels is part of the circulatory system.

items.q: Which level is the largest?
items.e: An organism is made of all its systems.

items.q: Which organ system does the pancreas (making insulin) belong to?
items.e: The pancreas (making insulin) is part of the endocrine system.

items.q: Which organ system does the skin belong to?
items.e: The skin is part of the integumentary system.

items.q: Which organ system does the biceps belong to?
items.e: The biceps is part of the muscular system.

items.q: What level comes right after organ (going from small to large)?
items.e: organ → organ system.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for controlling blood sugar after a meal?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Which list goes from smallest to largest?
c: cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
cell → tissue → organ system → organ → organism
cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
tissue → cell → organ → organ system → organism
items.e: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems.

items.q: What level is made of many cells working together?
items.e: Many cells make up a tissue.

items.q: Mark reads about a body system that collects information and sends messages that control the body. Which system is it?
items.e: The nervous system collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: Which level of organization is nerve tissue?
items.e: Nerve tissue is a tissue.

items.q: Kevin reads about a body system that moves the body by pulling on bones. Which system is it?
items.e: The muscular system moves the body by pulling on bones.

items.q: Which level of organization is the nervous system?
items.e: The nervous system is an organ system.

items.q: What level is made of many organs working together?
items.e: Many organs make up an organ system.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for fighting an infection carried in the blood?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Diane reads about a body system that removes wastes from the body. Which system is it?
items.e: The excretory system removes wastes from the body.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for getting oxygen to muscle cells?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: What level comes right after tissue (going from small to large)?
items.e: tissue → organ.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for breathing faster when you run?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Teeth chew a piece of bread into small pieces. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: Carbohydrase from the pancreas breaks starch into sugars. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: What does protease break proteins down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: Which food molecule does lipase break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: What is the job of the intercostal muscles?
c: A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Bones that protect the lungs and heart.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Amylase in saliva breaks starch into sugars. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: What is the job of the bronchioles?
c: Two tubes that carry air from the trachea into each lung.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches an alveolus (air sac)?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches a bronchus?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It absorbs water and mineral salts from undigested food.
items.e: The large intestine: It absorbs water and mineral salts from undigested food.

items.q: What is the job of the diaphragm?
c: A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.
Two tubes that carry air from the trachea into each lung.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It churns food and makes gastric juice with protease and acid to start digesting proteins.
items.e: The stomach: It churns food and makes gastric juice with protease and acid to start digesting proteins.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches a bronchiole?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which food molecule does protease break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: What is the main job of the mouth?
c: It moves food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis.
It stores faeces before they are removed from the body.
It makes pancreatic juice with carbohydrase, protease and lipase.
Teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts to digest starch.
items.e: The mouth: Teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts to digest starch.

items.q: The stomach walls churn food. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through the nose or mouth. Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Bones that protect the lungs and heart.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells?
items.e: A capillary carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.

items.q: What does a capillary do?
c: It carries blood back to the heart.
It carries blood away from the heart.
It carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.
items.e: A capillary carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.

items.q: A student counts 22 pulse beats in 10 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 22 × (60 ÷ 10).

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood back to the heart?
items.e: A vein carries blood back to the heart.

items.q: Blood is in the aorta. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Blood is in the right atrium. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
items.e: An artery carries blood away from the heart.

items.q: Which describes a vein?
c: It has a thick, muscular, elastic wall to withstand high pressure.
It has a thinner wall and valves to stop blood flowing backwards.
It has no wall at all.
It has a wall only one cell thick.
items.e: A vein has a thinner wall and valves to stop blood flowing backwards.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the lungs to the left atrium?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 72 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 80 cm³. What is the cardiac output in L per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 72 × 80 = 5,760 cm³/min.

items.q: Blood is in the left atrium. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: A student counts 12 pulse beats in 10 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 12 × (60 ÷ 10).

items.q: Blood is in the pulmonary vein. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Blood enters the pulmonary vein. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the body to the right atrium?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 150 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 60 cm³. What is the cardiac output in L per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 150 × 60 = 9,000 cm³/min.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the small intestine to the liver?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the left ventricle to the body?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Blood enters the right atrium. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the aorta to the kidney?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as transporting food from leaves?
items.e: Phloem: transporting food from leaves.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as the innermost layer of the cortex, with Casparian strips in roots?
items.e: Endodermis: the innermost layer of the cortex, with Casparian strips in roots.

items.q: Sugar made in the leaves is carried to the fruits of a durian tree. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Leaves have veins (xylem and phloem). How does this help the leaf?
c: Gases can move easily between the cells.
Carbon dioxide only has a short distance to diffuse to the cells.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
They open and close the stoma to control water loss.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Leaves are thin. How does this help the leaf?
c: Carbon dioxide only has a short distance to diffuse to the cells.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
They have a large surface area to absorb light.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Which description fits guard cells?
c: thin-walled living cells used for storage and photosynthesis
the layer just inside the endodermis that gives rise to lateral roots
a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss
cells that open and close the stomatal pore
items.e: Guard cells: cells that open and close the stomatal pore.

items.q: What does the vascular cambium produce?
c: secondary xylem on the inside and secondary phloem on the outside
items.e: This causes growth in girth.

items.q: What is the outermost layer of the primary plant body?
items.e: It is covered by cuticle in shoots.

items.q: Which tissue transports amino acids in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: What is endarch xylem?
c: protoxylem towards the center and metaxylem towards the outside
items.e: Found in stems; roots are exarch.

items.q: Food made in the leaves is stored in the tubers of a tapioca plant. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Mineral salts absorbed by the roots reach the leaves. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Which tissue transports water and mineral ions in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: Leaves are broad and flat. How does this help the leaf?
c: Carbon dioxide only has a short distance to diffuse to the cells.
They have a large surface area to absorb light.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
Gases can move easily between the cells.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Which description fits bulliform cells?
c: large empty cells in grass leaves that make them roll up in dry weather
conducting water and minerals from roots
parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem
openings in the bark for gas exchange
items.e: Bulliform cells: large empty cells in grass leaves that make them roll up in dry weather.

items.q: A rose in blue-colored water develops blue streaks in its petals. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Which description fits cuticle?
c: tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis
a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss
living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
cells that open and close the stomatal pore
items.e: Cuticle: a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss.

items.q: Which tissue transports sucrose in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem?
items.e: Medullary rays: parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem.

items.q: The upper surface has a waxy layer. How does this help the leaf?
c: They have a large surface area to absorb light.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.
